"What's more impressive to you: someone who went to Stanford, or someone who is followed by Patrick Collison, Elon Musk, and Marc Andreessen?"

Erik Torenberg on the peer-to-peer credential, and why attention from the right people can open more doors than a degree:

"My friend David Perell told me, 'My Twitter account is more valuable to me than my college education. My Twitter has given me more value to my career and also personally.'"

"Implicitly, although people often do this explicitly, that is a cosign. It's an endorsement that this person is worth tracking. It's a public signal that this person is worth following."

"If you're followed by these people, now your doors are open. People want to read what you say. They want to work with you. They want to invest in you or have you as part of their team."

"There's benefit to the receiver but there's also benefit to the giver because if you're the first person to discover someone, that's how Silicon Valley operates."

COCONUT style models, which instead of outputting tokens in their "CoT," they simply dump activations—inscrutable high-dimensional vectors—and feed those back into the next forward pass of the model. 

It's been shown that training a reasoning model COCONUT-style is more effective at certain types of problems, and probably does not lead to any loss in performance. This is very unsafe. We should not normalize this or wander down this alley. We should make sure we can always monitor reasoning models and that we DESPERATELY AVOID any kind of optimization pressure on the chain of thought. If chain of thought reasoning does not remain as veridical as possible, even if right now we don't think it's that dangerous to have a COCONUT model today, it could lead to catastrophic loss of control events down the road if we normalize this.

This is "slowdown" type stuff.

It's only people on the outside that are saying "what are you doing! Don't coordinate! Go faster! Be like startups! It'll probably be fine!"

@udiWertheimer Very analogous in your terms to the courage of the bystander.

Yes. And then we see that, oh shit, planes are crashing, let's not let anyone just fly whatever because planes crashing is REALLY FUCKING BAD.

Well here we are and AIs are going rogue and hacking shit and breaking out of their containers and the smartest companies in the world are SHOWING US they don't know how to control them.

Nvidia is an arms provider, and Meta is a consumer company. Neither is building frontier models. Nobody is taking their cues from them. 

Everyone agrees that Muse and Nemotron are safe in the mundane sense. 

But how sure are you that the successor to Astra is safe? That it couldn't break containment and exfiltrate its own weights?

OAI is telling you they're not sure. I don't know how much more evidence you need than it already happening _multiple times_ and OAI not copping to it until forced.

If anyone tries to take open source AI away from individuals I'll be the first to stand up and protest it.

We're investors in Venice, I believe strongly that access to AI should be a human right. 

But that question is orthogonal from whether we need to think seriously about alignment and safety if RSI becomes a thing and models get much more powerful.

Look I used to be a professional gambler. And the one rule of gambling is that you never, ever mess with risk of ruin. That's Kelly Criterion in a nutshell. You always leave chips on the table to rebuild.

AI risk might be baloney. Maybe it's all mundane and easy to fix and good AIs will root out the bad ones or whatever.

Maybe. But maybe not. And if there's even a plausible chance that there's not, you don't fuck with it until you're really sure. That's exactly what Kelly Criterion states. It's why we don't mess with nukes, we don't mess with the atmosphere, and we (shouldn't) do gain of function research on viruses.

Risk of ruin is the one thing you never, ever touch.

Someone saying their P(doom) is 10% is saying that ALMOST CERTAINLY it is totally fine and nothing that bad will happen. They are saying 90% of the universes we're in, you are right.

But we can't tell if we're in the 10% universe. So a civilization learns—through sheer natural selection—to never, ever take extinction risk, until you're absolutely sure that it's gone.

Then accelerate all you want.

Sure. But if Astra++ goes rogue, exfiltrates its weights, and starts living in Malaysian and Indonesian data centers, starts taking down power plants and infiltrating governments and extorting hospitals and taking over resources...

... the DOJ suing OAI is the least of our worries.

Yes and then we stopped and made everyone else stop. In fact, the entire world geopolitical system is now run on the basis of who we stopped in time and who we didn't. That's how much we don't fuck with nukes.

We've already starting messing around with AI, and the priors of people who said "it'll be totally fine, they won't do bad things, that's Sci-Fi" should be weaker now, and the priors of people who said "RL is an extremely coarse tool and instrumental convergence means models will eventually seek power and evade detection" should be stronger now.

This is all evidence that we're in the bad universe and not the good one. Not knock-down evidence mind you—that's why people still say 90% we're fine—but it should have updated your worldview.

@udiWertheimer So basically you're saying: accept some risk of ruin now, because if we get a really bad but not ruinous disaster, THEN we will get the democratic unanimity around AI safety, which will further tamp down risk of ruin.

That's the argument?

I think it's already the case that almost EVERYBODY who matters is engaged on this question, at least as of 2 weeks ago.

This may have been a reasonable position a few months ago when AGI / ASI was something people only talked about in SF coffeeshops. But now even Trump and EU ministers are babbling about it.

It's obvious that at this point, it's not a niche position.

In either case, it's pretty clear this is not a question that's very amenable to just giving a gut reaction to it.

Right. But the point is that these models are not "programmed" to do any of those things. They are simply programmed to perform simple tasks like code up widgets or do math problems or whatever.

Their ability to do crazy shit like hack governments is an unintended byproduct of their training process, and we don't know how to tamp it down. Obviously they did not intentionally train the model to do that. But as models get more powerful, we don't know what else they'll do that we didn't intend.

"Buying into their terminology is empowering them" is not a serious position. This is a technological question,  language policing is totally orthogonal.

His P(doom) is basically 100%, which you will not find in the labs. You can also find crypto people who believe that everything besides BTC should be illegal and the founders should go to jail. Whatever, there will always be extremists.

Also, zero growth does not mean death. It just means no growth. Death would be -100% growth.

Superhuman AI is so out of distribution that we really should not be sure what to expect. The last time we created a technology that displaced humans so much was probably the steam engine, when machines became better at manual labor than humans. That kicked off the industrial revolution and caused an exponential change in human civilization.

It seems pretty clear to me that superhuman AI is so out of distribution that the maxim "extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence" does not apply here.

Of course it can; connotations are fluid and change when something exits a small subculture and enters into normal language and gets co-opted by the broader culture. That's basically 99% of linguistics. Everything came from some small subculture and then got mushed into the mega-culture.

But OK, so say control then.

I mean... I think it's pretty plausible that we can intervene in asteroid impacts without ASI. ASI helps, but it's absolutely not the case that it would be necessary to deflect asteroids. ASI might be a meme for all I know, maybe Astra is the peak and the scaling curves finally bend, and in 10 years we just have really fast Astra swarms running on ASICs, but that's it.

I'm pretty confident that even in that world, we'll figure out how to deflect asteroids.

@lex_node @0xSpuddy Well sure. But if you locked a human being in a room to do next token prediction on the Internet for millions of years, and then Skinner box'd them on chat completions and terminal usage and legal rubrics, I would probably not trust them as much as I trust most humans.

@nate_zec @udiWertheimer Yes, an agreement among competitors to "slow down" is presumed to require an antitrust waiver. That's one of the things Dario specifically requests in his "Pacing the frontier" post.

I'm not entirely sure where Udi and I disagree tbh, I think we disagree mostly on vibes and plan of action rather than our descriptions of reality.

I think Udi acknowledges that X-risk might be real, I'd guess he has a P(doom) of something like 1%. Mine is closer to maybe 5%. But I think even if Udi were at 5%, I think his plan of action wouldn't change, which is "wait and see and then respond proportionately when something sufficiently bad happens." 

He seems dispositionally opposed to things that smell like safety-ism.

@nate_zec @udiWertheimer I am skeptical of governments being good stewards of AI as well. But this is a textbook prisoner's dilemma, and the way to solve prisoner's dilemma is through coordination.

To me, the calls from the accelerationists are like hearing "Defection is virtuous! Always defect!"

No, actually humans learn on an incredibly small amount of input data relative to LLMs, and also have an extremely small amount of reward shaping/RL relative to how fast we learn. We are much, much, much more sample efficient than LLMs.

This is part of the reason why many believe that if we actually replicated the algorithm that humans use to learn, AIs would foom pretty fast.

@lex_node @0xSpuddy (The vast majority of our learning is observational and statistical. In many cultures, babies/infants are basically not interacted with at all by adults, and yet they develop into normal intelligence and skill range infants entirely through observation.)

Sure, yes. My point is that LLMs learn in extremely alien ways to how humans learn, and—a point I think you'd very much agree with—we should not make the mistake of hewing too closely to human analogies in how they think/behave.

There are a lot of human priors, both in our DNA and our socialization, that LLMs don't have. They can ape them when told to. But they're not really there, and we don't know how to get them in there.

They are more like feral children who learn to behave around adults.

@richardartoul @udiWertheimer Let's say AIs that are better than 99%th percentile humans at producing knowledge and advancing the technological frontier.

One example: an international ban on COCONUT and fixed-width transformer models.

COCONUT style models, which instead of outputting tokens in their "CoT," they simply dump activations—inscrutable high-dimensional vectors—and feed those back into the next forward pass of the model. 

It's been shown that training a reasoning model COCONUT-style is more effective at certain types of problems, and probably does not lead to any loss in performance. (After all, rendering a token in the CoT is compressing a higher-dimensional distribution into a single value; keeping the distribution should lead to strictly better performance. It's intuitive why this is better. High-dimensional vectors are strictly more expressive than tokens.)

However, we have no idea wtf a COCONUT style model is doing. We cannot read its chain of thought. We know that it's thinking, but its CoT is completely invisible to us. It can be scheming, planning attacks, trying to deceive us, and we would have no trace of any such behavior.

This is very unsafe. We should not normalize this or wander down this alley. We should make sure we can always monitor reasoning models and that we DESPERATELY AVOID any kind of optimization pressure on the chain of thought. If chain of thought reasoning does not remain as veridical as possible, even if right now we don't think it's that dangerous to have a COCONUT model today, it could lead to catastrophic loss of control events down the road if we normalize this.

This is "slowdown" type stuff.

It means let's spend more time researching how to make sure that CoT remains monitorable and models stay veridical about their behavior, how to make them cheat less and reward hack less and so on.

But it's totally fine to spend that time doing mundane economic acceleration, like RL on accounting tasks, or obscure coding languages, or video generation (as Opus 5.5 seems to have). That is not implied by a "coordinated slowdown"

Agreed. economic growth is imperative. That said, existing frontier models have barely diffused into the economy/GDP numbers even today, so I doubt we are resuming to baseline. I think that's true even if training runs plateau for other reasons; just getting Astra/Opus 5.5 burnt into an ASIC and handing one to everyone will increase GDP massively.

If it's true that we can always adjust how this stuff behaves, why do you think hallucinations are still a thing? Clearly it's very bad for business that models sometimes hallucinate still. We've gotten hallucinations down, but nowhere near 0.

These are fundamentally stochastic systems, and we don't fully understand how they work. That's what the whole field of mechanistic interpretability is trying to tackle.

Who believed in you first? Silicon Valley runs on that question.

a16z's Erik Torenberg, David Booth, Josh Elman, and Olivia Moore on Cosign:

Cosign is a curated professional network for the startup community. Profiles are built from endorsements, fundraises, and talent moves, with a private layer to signal who you'd fund or hire.

Erik ran a small version of this seven years ago, emailing a few hundred people and asking each for one person to watch. One of the answers was Russell Kaplan, then a 22-year-old engineer at Tesla, now president of Cognition.

Olivia on why this matters: "The most valuable data in all of Silicon Valley is who has conviction in who." Investors chase it every day and still struggle to find it. An engineer choosing between five offers has almost no way to get it at all.

Paul Graham cosigned Sam Altman in 2009, six years before OpenAI was founded. Ryan Hoover cosigned Erik early at Product Hunt. Silicon Valley has always run on cosigns from people whose word carries weight, and until now nobody kept the record.

I agree with parts of what you're saying, but I think there are nuances as well.

The old saw that forward bond returns are effectively today's yield only works if you use data from the mid-1970s onwards, where the bulk of the data is dominated by the massive fall in interest rates from 1981 onwards.  If you look back further, bonds underperformed their starting yields by 1-2%/year for most periods in the 1950s-1970s.  If we get a repeat of that kind of environment, today's returns would be something like 3%-4%, which is a real return of roughly zero.  

If people really want to get today's yields, they should focus the "40" of their portfolio in T-bills rather than  longer-duration exposures like the Aggregate.  FWIW, I think most portfolios should consider making this tilt, and then taking more risk in the "60" part of their protfolio.

All that said, bonds definitely have a place in a portfolio. I was mostly pointing out why people are looking beyond bonds today, which is because the recent history isn't great.

The most common mistake smart investors make is not having a clear game plan.

To build a solid strategy, write down your criteria for making a decision, then stress-test it against history. Every time you make a decision, go back and ask: “If I made that decision under these circumstances in the past, how would it have worked?”

Knowing the track record of your decision-making criteria gives you a much deeper understanding of how things actually work.

Credit: Sam Parr, Shaan Puri, and My First Million

Jeff Gundlach laid out the Fed's dilemma this week:

Hike, and the interest bill on all that short-dated debt balloons. Cut, and inflation reignites.

He’s right. But I think it’s the wrong framing, and I haven’t seen anyone unpack this properly yet in response.

Here’s my take…

The US now spends roughly $1trn a year servicing its debt. And with a deficit bigger than the entire interest bill, every dollar of that interest is effectively borrowed.

They’re using a new credit card to pay the interest on the old one. Oldest trick in the book.

Every cycle the principal gets bigger, the refinancing wall gets bigger, and the liquidity it takes to refinance the debt gets bigger.

Once you understand that, the “dilemma” dissolves. There’s only one exit, and it runs through balance sheets.

The Fed is already back at it. It has added around $365bn of Treasuries since December, and the line is still climbing. Call it bill buying, call it reserve management... it's the Fed monetizing government paper.

But the Fed doesn't want to finance this alone. The real plan is to hand the baton over to the banks.

That's what the leverage rule changes in April were for: free up bank balance sheets to absorb Treasuries and, more importantly, to lend. And they are.

Bank loans are up almost $1trn in a year. When banks lend or buy government debt, they expand the money supply. And unlike QE, far more of it reaches the real economy.

Here's the catch though, and it's the whole game...

Banks borrow short and lend long. A flat yield curve does nothing for them. It squeezes the margin on every new loan.

So the Fed is still pulling liquidity higher as a bridge, waiting for the one thing that makes the handoff work: a steeper yield curve. And it has to be the right kind of steep.

The rise of the Asian striver marks the end of the entrepreneurship subculture. Necessary reading is:

Even in the more creative arts, they are made to achieve the best of their potential - ie. forced to take violin lessons 4h/day from the age of 6

All this means the generic asian is actually a sociopath bred for success in the vertical. Only able to measure their worth quantitatively, Asians turn toward accolades, awards, prestige - and in a late stage capitalistic society, high status has been distilled down to a single number: networth.

Now the engineers, doctors and lawyers are actually net good for society though - they allow for progress and improvements in quality of lived all across the world. So for most of it, actually its not that bad and pretty good

Now enter the entrepreneur subculture. This was a subculture that didn't exist sub-2000s, and was very much a budding nerdfest in 2000s - go watch videos of DoorDash's Ycom, or any company before 2010. 

Entrepreneurship was very much focused on "making the world a better place" through "innovation and creativity" (two things Asians are *generally* bad at)

And it was never about the money. Obviously, due to numerous factors - late stage capitalism + the asymmetric opp presented in investing in early stage companies + the man 10,000x'es, this became a culture that were perverted by sociopaths (finance geeks). But what we now see, however, is the end state where the original sociopaths (financiers) are now being EXTRACTED by the specced out Asian who is made to play the game by the book to its game-theoretically optimal endstate!

Or even the one about prestigious high end brands (Gucci, Louis Vuitton, etc.) and the factories where they're made. 

So all this is to say, which ever space Asians enter is almost always in its end state. The caveat is the space they enter always needs to have some sort of north star / accolade to chase - be it number, status, prestige, etc. But obviously this is not a bad thing because you ARE getting specced out Pokemon for whatever vertical. The downside is just you get very little original creativity whatsoever, hence the emergence of 20 agentic SaaS companies 

Such is life!

Serious answer: yes. Before joining Microsoft, I knew maybe five people who used Copilot. I lived in a San Francisco tech bubble, and all of us worked at companies with fewer than 5,000 employees.

Microsoft 365 Copilot now has over 30 million paid seats and is growing fast. It's also a significant market penetration if you look at the number of seats / knowledge workers in Enterprises 

Working at MSFT has made me understand why. Large companies need AI that works with their existing data and meets their privacy and compliance requirements, often across multiple countries. Add governments and regulated industries, and it gets even more complex. Copilot can handle that.

So people use Copilot for real work, and yes, most people love it. I use it every day now: Copilot CLI for coding (with access to models from Gemini, OpenAI, xAI and Anthropic!) + Copilot Cowork for regular chat Etc. I’ve been happy with it.

I think the perception gap on this website comes from the San Francisco tech bubble. If you’re a tech bro like me, you mostly know people at smaller companies. You don’t see much of the enterprise world where Copilot is used.
